screens.title: What goes wrong?
screens.text: Insert 3, then 2, then 1 into an empty AVL tree. What happens when 1 arrives?
options: Nothing happens, because the tree is still balanced
Node 3 gets a balance factor of −2
Node 1 gets a balance factor of −2
screens.answer: Node 3 gets a balance factor of −2
screens.reveal: Node 3 now has an empty right branch (height −1) and a left branch of height 1, so its balance factor is −1 − 1 = −2. This is Case 1, and a right rotation about 3 fixes it.

screens.title: Goal
screens.text: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to insert keys into an AVL tree and keep the AVL property after every insertion.

task.stem: Where does a new key go in a BST?
task.hint: This question checks whether you can place a new key. Search for it as in a BST, and it goes into the empty branch where the search ends.

options.text: At the root, and the old root moves down
options.explanation: BST insertion never changes the root. The new key always becomes a leaf.

options.text: In the empty branch where a search for it ends, so it becomes a new leaf
options.explanation: AVL insertion starts in exactly this way.

options.text: Next to the key that is closest in value, even if that node already has two children
options.explanation: The search continues until it reaches an empty branch, and the new key goes there.

screens.title: The insertion procedure
points: 1. Insert the key as in a BST.
2. Backtrack towards the root, updating the balance factors.
3. Stop at the first node n whose balance factor is below −1 or above +1.

4. Decide the case. If the balance factor of n is negative, the left branch is too tall. It is Case 2 (LR) if the new key is larger than n.left, and otherwise it is Case 1 (LL). If the balance factor is positive, it is Case 3 (RL) if the new key is smaller than n.right, and otherwise it is Case 4 (RR).
5. Rotate, and then stop. No ancestor of n needs its balance factor changed.
screens.showRule: Insert the key, backtrack, and stop at the first unbalanced node n. Then find the case and fix it once, with a single or a double rotation.

screens.title: Example 1 (fully worked)
screens.text: This is part 1 of the textbook's running example. Insert 3, 2 and 1, and then 4 to 7, into an empty AVL tree. You can check each step in the textbook.
steps: The tree is empty, so 3 becomes the root.
2 is smaller than 3, so the search goes left.
2 goes into the empty left branch of 3.
Node 3 now has a balance factor of −1 − 0 = −1.
1 is smaller than 3, so the search goes left.
1 is smaller than 2, so the search goes left.
1 goes into the empty left branch of 2.
Node 2 now has a balance factor of −1 − 0 = −1.
Node 3 now has a balance factor of −1 − 1 = −2.
Node 3 has a balance factor of −2, so it is the first unbalanced node, n. This is Case 1 (LL).
Rotate 2 around 3. This is a right rotation about 3.
Every node now has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.
4 is larger than 2, so the search goes right.
4 is larger than 3, so the search goes right.
4 goes into the empty right branch of 3.
Node 3 now has a balance factor of 0 − (−1) = +1.
Node 2 now has a balance factor of 1 − 0 = +1.
5 is larger than 2, so the search goes right.
5 is larger than 3, so the search goes right.
5 is larger than 4, so the search goes right.
5 goes into the empty right branch of 4.
Node 4 now has a balance factor of 0 − (−1) = +1.
Node 3 now has a balance factor of 1 − (−1) = +2.
Node 3 has a balance factor of +2, so it is the first unbalanced node, n. This is Case 4 (RR).
Rotate 4 around 3. This is a left rotation about 3.
Every node now has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.
6 is larger than 2, so the search goes right.
6 is larger than 4, so the search goes right.
6 is larger than 5, so the search goes right.
6 goes into the empty right branch of 5.
Node 5 now has a balance factor of 0 − (−1) = +1.
Node 4 now has a balance factor of 1 − 0 = +1.
Node 2 now has a balance factor of 2 − 0 = +2.
Node 2 has a balance factor of +2, so it is the first unbalanced node, n. This is Case 4 (RR).
Rotate 4 around 2. This is a left rotation about 2.
Every node now has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.
7 is larger than 4, so the search goes right.
7 is larger than 5, so the search goes right.
7 is larger than 6, so the search goes right.
7 goes into the empty right branch of 6.
Node 6 now has a balance factor of 0 − (−1) = +1.
Node 5 now has a balance factor of 1 − (−1) = +2.
Node 5 has a balance factor of +2, so it is the first unbalanced node, n. This is Case 4 (RR).
Rotate 6 around 5. This is a left rotation about 5.
Every node now has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.

screens.title: Example 2 (guided)
screens.text: In part 2, insert 16, 15 and 14. At each imbalance, the app pauses and asks you to click n and name the case before it continues.
steps: 16 is larger than 4, so the search goes right.
16 is larger than 6, so the search goes right.
16 is larger than 7, so the search goes right.
16 goes into the empty right branch of 7.
Node 7 now has a balance factor of 0 − (−1) = +1.
Node 6 now has a balance factor of 1 − 0 = +1.
Node 4 now has a balance factor of 2 − 1 = +1.
15 is larger than 4, so the search goes right.
15 is larger than 6, so the search goes right.
15 is larger than 7, so the search goes right.
15 is smaller than 16, so the search goes left.
15 goes into the empty left branch of 16.
Node 16 now has a balance factor of −1 − 0 = −1.
Node 7 now has a balance factor of 1 − (−1) = +2.
Node 7 has a balance factor of +2, so it is the first unbalanced node, n. This is Case 3 (RL).
Rotate 15 around 16. This is a right rotation about 16.
Rotate 15 around 7. This is a left rotation about 7.
Every node now has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.
14 is larger than 4, so the search goes right.
14 is larger than 6, so the search goes right.
14 is smaller than 15, so the search goes left.
14 is larger than 7, so the search goes right.
14 goes into the empty right branch of 7.
Node 7 now has a balance factor of 0 − (−1) = +1.
Node 15 now has a balance factor of 0 − 1 = −1.
Node 6 now has a balance factor of 2 − 0 = +2.
Node 6 has a balance factor of +2, so it is the first unbalanced node, n. This is Case 3 (RL).
Rotate 7 around 15. This is a right rotation about 15.
Rotate 7 around 6. This is a left rotation about 6.
Every node now has a balance factor of −1, 0 or +1.

screens.title: Example 3 (on your own)
screens.text: In part 3, insert 13, 12, 11 and 10, one at a time. After each one, build the rebalanced tree.

task.stem: Insert 13, 12, 11 and 10, one at a time, and rebalance after each insertion.
task.hint: This question checks the whole insertion. Insert the key as in a BST, update the balance factors on the way up, and then fix the first unbalanced node with the rotation or rotations for its case.

feedback.correct: Inserting 13 gives Case 4 at 4, 12 gives Case 1 at 14, 11 gives Case 1 at 15, and 10 gives Case 1 at 12. Each fix is a single rotation.
feedback.incorrect: Inserting 13 gives Case 4 at 4, 12 gives Case 1 at 14, 11 gives Case 1 at 15, and 10 gives Case 1 at 12. Each fix is a single rotation.

task.stem: Insert 8 and then 9, and rebalance after each insertion.
task.hint: This question checks the whole insertion. Insert the key as in a BST, update the balance factors on the way up, and then fix the first unbalanced node with the rotation or rotations for its case.

feedback.correct: 8 needs no rotation. 9 makes node 10 unbalanced, with a balance factor of −2. 9 is between 8 and 10, so it went into the right subtree of the left child of 10, which is Case 2. The fix is a left rotation about 8, followed by a right rotation about 10.
feedback.incorrect: 8 needs no rotation. 9 makes node 10 unbalanced, with a balance factor of −2. 9 is between 8 and 10, so it went into the right subtree of the left child of 10, which is Case 2. The fix is a left rotation about 8, followed by a right rotation about 10.

screens.title: Why one fix is enough
screens.caption: Before 1 was inserted, the subtree rooted at 3 had height 1. After the insertion and the right rotation, the subtree, which is now rooted at 2, has height 1 again. Because the fixed subtree is as tall as before, nothing above it changes.

screens.title: Lesson check
screens.text: This check has one question for each assessment criterion of the lesson's objective. You can re-attempt each question once, and the Hint button is always available.

screens.title: Summary
points: Insert the key as in a BST, and then walk back up, updating the balance factors.
Fix only the first unbalanced node n, using the rotation or rotations for its case.
One fix is enough, because the subtree gets back its old height.
